title: Why land-use emissions have fallen by a third this century – in six charts - Carbon Brief
gist: Global land-use-change emissions have fallen roughly a third since the 2000s, driven mainly by declining deforestation in Brazil, peatland rewetting in Indonesia and reforestation in China, even as fossil-fuel and cement emissions hit new records. The decline is concentrated in a few export-driven tropical economies where international trade regulations bite, while the DRC's subsistence-driven emissions keep rising.

themes.theme: Land-use emissions trajectory vs fossil emissions

insights.claim: Global land-use-change emissions averaged 5GtCO2 a year over 2015-24, around 23% lower than the 1995-2004 average and 19% lower than 2005-14, while land-use emissions in 2025 fell to about 32% below their 2000s average.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: A structural downtrend in land-use emissions offsets part of fossil growth, tempering the pace of atmospheric CO2 accumulation relevant to carbon-price and offset markets.
insights.quote: land-use emissions in 2025 had decreased by “around 32% compared to their average in the 2000s”

insights.claim: Fossil-fuel and cement emissions have risen every decade since 1959, from about 11GtCO2 in the 1960s to 35.9GtCO2 over 2015-24, with preliminary 2025 data reaching a new high of 38.1GtCO2 as land-use emissions fell to 4.1GtCO2.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Fossil emissions remain the dominant, still-growing driver; land-use gains are not offsetting continued fossil demand growth for energy and commodity markets.
insights.quote: fossil-fuel and cement emissions reached a new high of 38.1GtCO2

insights.claim: In the four decades to 1999, net CO2 emissions from land-use change stayed relatively constant at around 6.6GtCO2 per year before beginning a statistically significant decline in the late 1990s.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Establishes the pre-decline baseline needed to size the magnitude of the trend for carbon-budget and net-zero pathway modelling.

insights.claim: Falling land-use emissions since the late 1990s are attributed to decreasing deforestation, especially permanent deforestation, combined with increasing CO2 removals from forest regrowth.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Identifies which policy and land-management levers actually move the trend, informing where deforestation-linked commodity and offset value concentrates.

insights.claim: Over 2015-24 forest growth removed 4.76GtCO2 a year, offsetting two-thirds of the 6.96GtCO2 average annual deforestation emissions, with 2.2GtCO2 from afforestation and reforestation and 2.56GtCO2 from shifting-cultivation regrowth.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Quantifies the gross sink offsetting deforestation, sizing the physical basis for forest-carbon-removal supply relevant to CDR and offset pricing.

insights.claim: The steep post-2015 drop in land-use emissions is attributed to a 2015 peak in peat fire emissions combined with a long-term decline in deforestation emissions across many countries over 2010-20.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Distinguishes a one-off fire peak from a durable deforestation trend, important for judging whether the decline is structural or cyclical.

insights.claim: The projected 2024-to-2025 drop in land-use emissions is attributed to the end of El Nino conditions, which typically dry out tropical peatlands and cause planned deforestation fires to burn out of control.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Links ENSO cycles to year-to-year emissions volatility, a signal for anticipating land-use emission swings tied to climate oscillations.

insights.claim: There is no clear indication of future land-use emissions trends, but under current global land policies the assumption is that deforestation should continue to decline.
insights.speaker: Pierre Friedlingstein
insights.so_what: The lead scientist explicitly flags forecast uncertainty, cautioning against extrapolating the recent decline in net-zero scenarios.
insights.quote: If you are optimistic, you hope the trend will not reverse and start increasing again. But we don’t know for sure.

insights.claim: Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Indonesia together contributed 57% of global land-use emissions over 2015-24.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Land-use emission risk is highly concentrated in three tropical economies, focusing where deforestation-linked supply-chain and sovereign policy risk sits.
insights.locator: Which countries are behind falling land-use emissions?

insights.claim: The decline in global land-use emissions since the 2000s has been primarily driven by falling deforestation in Brazil, where tree clearance peaked in the 2000s and fell under forest-protection policies despite politically driven fluctuations between the Lula and Bolsonaro administrations.
insights.speaker: Pierre Friedlingstein
insights.so_what: Brazilian domestic politics is the swing factor for the global land-use trend, making election cycles a material variable for soy/beef supply chains and forest-carbon markets.
insights.quote: the long-term trend in Brazil is a decline in deforestation due to forest protection policies

insights.claim: Brazil's deforestation decline was driven by concrete measures including a 2004 Amazon deforestation action plan, a 2006 soy moratorium banning purchase and financing of soya from deforested Amazon areas, and expansion of protected areas in the late 2000s.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Trade-linked commodity restrictions, not just protected areas, drove the result, showing supply-chain regulation as a lever affecting agricultural export flows.

insights.claim: Indonesia is the largest contributor to the past decade's acceleration in declining land-use emissions, having rewetted more peatland area since 2017 alone than Europe has in its entire history.
insights.speaker: Julia Pongratz
insights.so_what: Peatland rewetting is a scalable, high-impact mitigation lever that materially shifts the global figure, relevant to nature-based carbon-credit supply.
insights.quote: rewetted more peatland area since 2017 alone than Europe in its entire history

insights.claim: Emissions in the DRC have increased and stayed high over the last two decades because deforestation there is driven by population growth and expanding smallholder subsistence farming rather than export, making international trade regulations less effective than in Brazil and Indonesia.
insights.speaker: Julia Pongratz
insights.so_what: Trade-based deforestation policy fails where drivers are domestic subsistence, signaling a persistent emissions source that export-focused regulation cannot address.
insights.quote: international regulations aiming at curbing deforestation thus have larger effects in these countries

insights.claim: China, the EU and US account for the highest levels of reforestation and afforestation carbon sequestration, collectively drawing down 1.1GtCO2 per year over 2015-24, partly a legacy of 19th- and 20th-century forest transitions.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Developed-economy forest sinks are a large, quantified drawdown pool, relevant to how national inventories and CDR accounting credit legacy regrowth.
insights.locator: Which countries are leading on forest regrowth?

insights.claim: China's 1990s reforestation and land-management policies rehabilitated tens of millions of hectares of forest, driving its land-use emissions below zero and switching its land from a carbon source to a carbon sink.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: A national-scale afforestation program can flip a country to net land-carbon removal, a template and benchmark for state-directed CDR policy.

insights.claim: The Global Carbon Budget's average annual land-use emissions figure for 2015-24 carries an uncertainty range of 2.6GtCO2 per year, more than half the 5GtCO2 central estimate, and is derived by averaging three bookkeeping models: BLUE, OSCAR and LUCE.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: The signal-to-noise on land-use data is weak, meaning carbon-budget accounting built on these figures carries large embedded error for policy and market use.
insights.locator: Why are estimates of land-use emissions uncertain?

insights.claim: Confidence in the 2025 land-use emissions projection is rated low because it relies on deforestation, degradation and peat-fire proxies, with 2023 the last year emissions are calculated directly from full land-use statistics across all three models.
insights.speaker: Cecilia Keating
insights.so_what: Recent-year figures are proxy-based and revisable, so near-term emission headlines should be treated as provisional signals.
insights.locator: Why are estimates of land-use emissions uncertain?
